_source: Branch Education long video 'How do Video Game Graphics Work?' (owner's favourite reference), watched in the built-in browser 2026-11-18: 77 s played straight with the audio probe and frames every ~7 s, then frames every 2-5 s to 125 s, 0.4-0.5 s bursts at 21-23 s, 212-213 s and 345-346 s, and one frame every 30-80 s to the end. Sentence timings and word counts from the transcript panel (not kept; timestamps are per caption block). After 125 s the shots and lines are one per chapter, with what the sampled frames showed. Our own descriptions.

hook.firstFrame: a dim gamer's desk at night lit in teal and pink: a monitor, a console, shelves of game machines
hook.firstLine: Games now show breathtaking worlds and cities in huge detail

shots.picture: a gamer's desk at night in teal light; the camera pushes toward the monitor where game clips play
slanted panels of different game clips slide past the camera like cards
gameplay clip: a rider walks toward a small railway station
the same station rebuilt as the channel's own 3D scene with a steam locomotive, daylight
the scene turns into glowing blue wireframe; a vertex counter ticks up beside the station
the wireframe fills in as white untextured clay; a triangle count appears
colours and textures paint back onto the station; a sun lights it
dark screen with streams of blue ones and zeros raining down
the graphics card's cooler lifts away to show the chip on its board
a game console, a handheld and a graphics card lined up on a dark studio floor
the card exploded into layers, glowing data streams flowing up into its chip
quick montage of gameplay clips
the graphics card on a dark floor; a green glowing line draws in from the left
glowing green lines like a metro map with nodes; step names write on in blue beside each node
a cloud of game cover cards floats over the three step names
the station scene from above, then shrinking into a panel
the scene sits as a framed panel in a dark blue grid world; objects outside the view drop away
close on the dark blue steam locomotive in studio light, then as mesh
a green camera icon projects a frustum onto a grid view screen; a mesh object sits beyond
a barrel in the frustum under a 3-stop timeline; transform matrices write on at the right
shots.onScreenText: Model Space, World Space, Camera Space

shots.picture: a glass view-screen plane with the scene projected on it and a vertex count
graphics card pulled apart; the chip die with a core count ticking up
a pixel grid with one white triangle; corner coordinates label each vertex
the station shown as a greyscale depth image, then game frames with overlapping objects
the locomotive lit by a bank of golden light rays; normals as small arrows over a red surface; street lamps at night
the sponsor's lesson screens on a dark backdrop
close on the locomotive boiler, flat versus smooth shaded
a classroom game scene with a soft, light-bounced look and a title
a game frame on a dark panel with labelled core types and a milliseconds-per-frame gauge
supporter credits in columns on a dark blue sky

lines.gist: games now show breathtaking, detailed worlds
a familiar game scene is really millions of points, triangles and textures under a virtual sun
all of it is just ones and zeros crunched by your graphics card
asks how the computer turns those bits into realistic 3D
names the three steps of the rendering pipeline
these steps have powered nearly every game for decades
step one moves every object onto the flat screen using the camera's view
one locomotive followed vertex by vertex through three coordinate changes
the GPU's thousands of cores do this maths in milliseconds
rasterization: which screen pixels each triangle covers
how the depth buffer decides what is hidden behind what
fragment shading: colour each pixel from lights, angles and textures, with the vector maths
the maths behind it, then the sponsor
flat versus smooth shading, and an appreciation of game artists
newer tricks: ray tracing, AI upscaling and the special cores that run them
future videos and thanks to supporters

ending.lastFrame: supporter credits in columns on a dark blue sky

whyItWorks: the hook takes a scene viewers know from a real game and peels it live: textured, then glowing wireframe with a counter, then white clay, then colour
one object (a locomotive) is followed through every step, so each abstract stage happens to the same familiar thing
big counts tick up as thin floating labels pinned to the 3D scene instead of separate number cards
chapters open on a pipeline map of glowing lines and nodes, so the viewer always knows where they are
